## In 60 seconds

Conduction velocity is the inverse of the activation-time gradient: $\mathbf v = \nabla T/\lvert\nabla T\rvert^2$. Every
estimator differs in how it gets $\nabla T$, and all of them inherit timing error. For two points $h$ apart, the
relative speed error is $\sqrt2\,\sigma c/h$, so fast conduction and close points make speed noisy; 1 ms of error at
1 m/s over 4 mm is 35%. **Triangulation** uses three points and is as good as the pair for an equilateral triangle, but
much worse for a thin one. A **local plane fit** to the $n$ points within radius $R$ cuts the noise to about
$2\sigma/(R\sqrt n)$ per component, at the cost of bias where activation curves. Because speed is an inverse, noise
in the gradient also biases speed low. **Potential-based (omnipolar)** methods skip activation times: for a plane
wave, $-\phi_t\nabla\phi/\lvert\nabla\phi\rvert^2$ is exact for any waveform, but a finite clique of electrodes biases it,
by an amount that grows with spacing over electrode height.

## From the field

- **Fitting surfaces to activation times.** Bayly and colleagues fitted local polynomial surfaces $T(x, y)$ to
  activation times and took speed and direction from their gradient. They validated this on simulations, then used it
  on pig epicardial recordings from arrays of over 500 electrodes [@bayly1998].
- **Speed differs with tissue voltage.** In one left-atrial study, conduction velocity averaged about 1.0 m/s in
  normal-voltage areas of the anterior wall and 0.6 m/s in low-voltage areas [@heil2023].
- **Velocity vectors in tachycardia maps.** In 20 patients with complex atrial tachycardias, a mapping method that
  built velocity vectors from delays between neighboring sites identified isthmus or breakout sites where ablation
  terminated the tachycardia in 25 of 26 tachycardias (96.2%), against 69.2% for conventional maps, as the study
  reports [@vicera2020].

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $T$ activation time; $\mathbf g = \nabla T$; $\mathbf v$ velocity; $c$ speed; $\sigma$ timing
SD; $\sigma_g$ gradient SD per component; $h$ point spacing; $E$ edge matrix of a triangle; $S$ covariance pattern of
time differences; $X_c$ centered coordinates; $n$ number of points; $R$ fit radius; $\phi$ potential; $\phi_t$ its time
derivative; $U$, $a$ the m03 waveform and its length scale; $d$ clique spacing.

### Speed from a gradient

$$
\mathbf v = \frac{\nabla T}{\lvert\nabla T\rvert^2}, \qquad c = \frac{1}{\lvert\nabla T\rvert}, \qquad \mathrm E\lvert\hat{\mathbf g}\rvert^2 = \lvert\mathbf g\rvert^2 + 2\sigma_g^2 \text{ (2D)}
$$ {#eq-m25-gradient}

Noise inflates the gradient on average, so speeds read low, and because speed is an inverse, the spread grows with
speed. With an illustrative gradient noise of 0.2 ms/mm, a true 1.0 m/s read 0.78–1.30 m/s (10th–90th percentile) and a
true 2.0 m/s read 1.27–3.35 m/s (lab part A).

### Two points and triangles

$$
\frac{\sigma_c}{c} = \frac{\sqrt2\,\sigma\,c}{h}
$$ {#eq-m25-pair}

$$
E = \begin{pmatrix} (\mathbf x_2 - \mathbf x_1)^\top \\ (\mathbf x_3 - \mathbf x_1)^\top \end{pmatrix}, \qquad E\,\mathbf g = \begin{pmatrix} T_2 - T_1 \\ T_3 - T_1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf g}) = \sigma^2 E^{-1} S E^{-\top}, \quad S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
$$ {#eq-m25-triangle}

Both follow by first-order error propagation. With 1 ms of timing error at 1.0 m/s, points 2 mm apart gave 71% relative
error and 8 mm apart 18%. An equilateral triangle of side $h$ has isotropic gradient SD $\sqrt2\,\sigma/h$, the same as
the pair; a 4-mm sliver 0.4 mm high had 3.06 ms/mm across its short side against 0.35 ms/mm (lab part B). Triangulation
is one of the standard methods reviewed by Cantwell and colleagues [@cantwell2015].

::: {.demo #m25-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m25-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m25-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m25-d1-noise.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: independent timing errors of equal SD; first-order propagation for two points or an equilateral triangle
  (@eq-m25-pair, @eq-m25-triangle) and for a least-squares plane over a uniformly filled disk (@eq-m25-planefit). Tested
  against `epml.velocity`.
- Parameters: default speed 1.0 m/s [@heil2023]; timing error and number of points are illustrative and adjustable.
- What it ignores: bias from curved activation (lab part C), position errors (m16–m19), and the breakdown of the
  first-order formulas when errors are large.
:::

### Local plane fits

$$
\hat{\mathbf g} = \arg\min_{\mathbf g, t_0}\sum_i\bigl(T_i - t_0 - \mathbf g\cdot\mathbf x_i\bigr)^2, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf g}) = \sigma^2(X_c^\top X_c)^{-1} \approx \Bigl(\frac{2\sigma}{R\sqrt n}\Bigr)^2 I \text{ for a disk}
$$ {#eq-m25-planefit}

More points and a larger radius reduce noise, but a large radius averages over curved activation. 10 mm from a focal
source, with dense illustrative sampling and 1 ms of error, the RMS speed error was 0.23 m/s at $R$ = 2.5 mm, 0.04 m/s
at 6 mm and 0.08 m/s at 9 mm, where bias dominated (lab part C). Bayly and colleagues fitted polynomial surfaces,
which can follow some of that curvature [@bayly1998].

### Potential-based (omnipolar) velocity

For a plane wave $\phi(\mathbf x, t) = U(\hat n\cdot\mathbf x - ct)$ of any waveform $U$:

$$
\mathbf v = -\frac{\phi_t\,\nabla\phi}{\lvert\nabla\phi\rvert^2}, \qquad \frac{\hat c}{c} = 1 + \frac{(d/2)^2}{a^2} \text{ for a cross-shaped clique at the front's arrival along an axis}
$$ {#eq-m25-omnipolar}

The first result needs no activation times. It is the idea behind the m03 clique velocity
([eq-m03-clique-velocity](m03-electrograms.qmd#eq-m03-clique-velocity)) and behind omnipolar methods, as described
by Massé, Deno, Magtibay and colleagues [@masse2016; @deno2017; @magtibay2019]. In practice $\nabla\phi$ comes
from differences between electrodes. For the cross-shaped clique here, with the m03 waveform, a 2-mm clique at 1 mm
height read speed 1.59 times too fast. At 40° to the axis it read 1.30 times, with the direction biased toward the
diagonal (lab part D). Other stencils and time windows have other biases.

::: {.demo #m25-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m25-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m25-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m25-d2-clique.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the m03 plane wave; a center electrode for $\phi_t$ and four electrodes at $\pm d/2$ along two axes for the
  gradient by central differences, evaluated as the front reaches the center (@eq-m25-omnipolar). Tested against
  `epml.velocity`.
- Parameters: speed 1.0 m/s [@heil2023]; front width 0.3 mm (m03); height 1 mm by default [@riccio2021]; spacing and
  angle adjustable.
- What it ignores: the field-loop and fitting steps of published omnipolar methods, other clique shapes, curved fronts
  and noise.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Speed is noisy where it is fast and where points are close; average gradients, not speeds.
- Every estimator trades noise for bias through its spacing or radius.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Conduction velocity maps are used to look for slow conduction, which tends to occur in
low-voltage tissue [@heil2023]. Velocity vectors from neighboring sites have been used in atrial tachycardia maps
[@vicera2020]. Omnipolar methods estimate velocity from potentials in a grid of electrodes [@magtibay2019]. Every
such estimate depends on timing error, point spacing and the estimator (@eq-m25-pair, @eq-m25-planefit).

**What the evidence is.** A methods paper with animal data [@bayly1998], a review of algorithms [@cantwell2015], an
observational clinical series [@vicera2020], a clinical study of regional velocities [@heil2023] and a review of
omnipolar methods [@magtibay2019].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Which estimator, over what spacing or radius?** (@eq-m25-triangle, @eq-m25-planefit)
- **What timing error, and how fast is conduction there?** (@eq-m25-pair)
- **Were speeds averaged, or gradients?** (@eq-m25-gradient)
- **For clique-based velocity, what clique size and height?** (@eq-m25-omnipolar)

## How experts think

Before trusting a conduction velocity, ask:

1. **How big is the timing error compared with the travel time between points?** (@eq-m25-pair)
2. **What shape are the triangles?** (@eq-m25-triangle)
3. **How large is the fit radius compared with the curvature of activation?** (@eq-m25-planefit)
4. **Was the speed averaged as an inverse of noisy gradients?** (@eq-m25-gradient)
5. **For potential-based velocity, how big is the clique compared with the electrode height?** (@eq-m25-omnipolar)

One sentence to keep: **speed is an inverse; noise makes fast conduction look erratic and slow regions look slow.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Gradient (@eq-m25-gradient) | $\mathbf v = \nabla T/\lvert\nabla T\rvert^2$; $\mathrm E\lvert\hat g\rvert^2 = \lvert g\rvert^2 + 2\sigma_g^2$ |
| Two points (@eq-m25-pair) | $\sigma_c/c = \sqrt2\,\sigma c/h$ |
| Triangle (@eq-m25-triangle) | $E\mathbf g = \Delta T$; $\operatorname{Cov} = \sigma^2E^{-1}SE^{-\top}$ |
| Plane fit (@eq-m25-planefit) | $\operatorname{Cov} = \sigma^2(X_c^\top X_c)^{-1} \approx (2\sigma/(R\sqrt n))^2 I$ |
| Potential (@eq-m25-omnipolar) | $\mathbf v = -\phi_t\nabla\phi/\lvert\nabla\phi\rvert^2$; cross clique $\hat c/c = 1 + (d/2)^2/a^2$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| About 1.0 m/s in normal-voltage and 0.6 m/s in low-voltage left atrium | @heil2023 |
| Isthmus or breakout sites identified in 96.2% vs 69.2% of 26 tachycardias (20 patients) | @vicera2020 |
| Polynomial surface fitting; 500-plus-electrode arrays | @bayly1998 |
| Timing and gradient errors, point counts, radii, geometry | illustrative |
| Relative errors, covariances, RMS errors, clique ratios | our own code |

## Practice questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In your answer, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. How do you get conduction velocity from an activation map?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\mathbf v = \nabla T/\lvert\nabla T\rvert^2$; speed is the inverse of the gradient magnitude (@eq-m25-gradient).

</details>

**Q2. Why does noise bias speed low?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Noise adds to the gradient's magnitude on average, $\mathrm E\lvert\hat g\rvert^2 = \lvert g\rvert^2 + 2\sigma_g^2$, and speed is
its inverse (@eq-m25-gradient).

</details>

**Q3. Two points 4 mm apart, 1 ms timing error each, 1 m/s. Relative speed error?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\sqrt2 \times 1 \times 1/4 \approx$ 35% (@eq-m25-pair).

</details>

**Q4. Why is fast conduction harder to measure?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The travel time between points is short compared with the timing error; relative error grows in proportion to
$c$ (@eq-m25-pair).

</details>

**Q5. How do you compute a gradient from three points, and when is it unreliable?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Solve $E\mathbf g = \Delta T$; the covariance $\sigma^2E^{-1}SE^{-\top}$ blows up for thin triangles (@eq-m25-triangle)
[@cantwell2015].

</details>

**Q6. What does a local plane fit buy you?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Averaging: gradient SD about $2\sigma/(R\sqrt n)$; but a large radius biases the estimate where activation
curves (@eq-m25-planefit) [@bayly1998].

</details>

**Q7. How would you choose the fit radius?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Balance noise, which falls with radius, against curvature bias, which grows; test on simulated data with known
speed (@eq-m25-planefit).

</details>

**Q8. How can a clique of electrodes estimate velocity without activation times?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For a plane wave, $\mathbf v = -\phi_t\nabla\phi/\lvert\nabla\phi\rvert^2$ for any waveform; a clique supplies $\nabla\phi$ and
$\phi_t$ (@eq-m25-omnipolar) [@masse2016; @deno2017].

</details>

**Q9. What limits the clique estimate?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Finite differences over spacing $d$ misestimate $\nabla\phi$ by order $(d/a)^2$; curved fronts and noise add
more (@eq-m25-omnipolar).

</details>

**Q10. You average speeds over a region with noisy gradients. What goes wrong?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Speed is an inverse; a few small noisy gradients give huge speeds that dominate the mean. Average gradients, or use
medians (@eq-m25-gradient).

</details>

**Q11. What speeds were reported for normal- and low-voltage left atrium in one study?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

About 1.0 m/s and 0.6 m/s [@heil2023].

</details>

**Q12. Name three families of conduction velocity estimators.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Triangulation and finite differences of activation times, local surface fitting, and potential-based (omnipolar)
methods (@eq-m25-triangle, @eq-m25-planefit, @eq-m25-omnipolar) [@cantwell2015].

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. Gradient 2 ms/mm. Speed?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.5 mm/ms = 0.5 m/s (@eq-m25-gradient).

</details>

**S2. Double the spacing between two points. Relative speed error?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Halved (@eq-m25-pair).

</details>

**S3. Same spacing, speed doubles. Relative error?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Doubled (@eq-m25-pair).

</details>

**S4. A plane fit uses 4 times as many points over the same disk. Gradient SD?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Halved (@eq-m25-planefit).

</details>

**S5. Cross clique, d = 2 mm, a = 2 mm, along an axis. Speed ratio?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1 + 1/4 =$ 1.25 (@eq-m25-omnipolar).

</details>

**S6. Gradient 1 ms/mm with noise SD 0.5 ms/mm per component. RMS gradient magnitude?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\sqrt{1 + 0.5} \approx$ 1.22 ms/mm (@eq-m25-gradient).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Velocity vector fields.** Bayly and colleagues' vector fields from polynomial surface fits during pacing and
  fibrillation [@bayly1998]. This module: local plane fits.
- **Algorithm comparison.** Cantwell and colleagues' overview of annotation and velocity methods [@cantwell2015]. This
  module: two points and triangles.
- **Omnipolar velocity.** Magtibay and colleagues' illustrations of omnipolar activation vectors [@magtibay2019]. This
  module: potential-based velocity.
